Launch With Us
Our Mission

Building India's First Reusable Small-Lift Rocket

Not a paper rocket. Not a rendering. A vehicle family we're testing, flying, and rebuilding — piece by piece, from a garage in Delhi to a launch pad.

SKYLX-S · SKYLX-M · SKYLX-HEthanol / LOXDelhi, India

India can put satellites in orbit. What it can't yet do is put small satellites in orbit cheap — reliably, on schedule, for under ₹40 crore. That gap is where SkyLakes lives.

We're building the SKYLX family — S, M, and H — a line of reusable small-lift launch vehicles designed to make sub-₹40Cr LEO access normal instead of exceptional. Not by out-funding the incumbents, but by out-testing them: cheaper iterations, faster failure, more flights per rupee.

Why This, Why Now

Open, legal, and almost entirely unbuilt

India's space sector just opened up. IN-SPACe exists. Private launch is legal, encouraged, and still almost entirely unbuilt. A handful of companies are chasing the top of the market — bigger payloads, bigger rockets, bigger checks. Almost nobody is building for the small satellite operators who need a ride to orbit and can't afford to wait in line behind a national mission.

That's the seat we're taking. Small-lift. Reusable. Priced for the customer who currently has no good option.

How We Build

Test-first, not paper-first

Every subsystem earns its place through hardware, not slides. Our LX-1 engine program didn't jump straight to a metal print — we ran a PLA-CF nozzle through water flow testing first, validating cooling channel geometry before committing to an expensive IN718 build. That's the philosophy end to end: de-risk cheap, commit expensive.

Propulsion

LX-1 Engine

LX-1 is our primary engine — ethanol/LOX, regeneratively cooled. We picked ethanol over kerosene after genuinely interrogating the trade, because it fits the mission profile we're building for.

Avionics

STM32F411 + Pi Zero 2W

A dual flight-computer architecture, stress-tested through a formal bare-metal-vs-Linux evaluation protocol run in shadow mode — because the flight computer doesn't get a second chance to be right.

Simulation

SimCore

We're building SimCore, our own flight simulation platform, to eventually get us off MATLAB/Simulink entirely. If it's core to how we fly, we want to own it.

Design & Iteration

Fusion 360 · Blender · KeyShot

Every airframe and engine gets modeled, visualized, and pressure-tested digitally before it touches a test stand — iterated the same way we iterate hardware: fast, and without ego.

The Roadmap

How we get there

We're not pretending a small team in Delhi ships a reusable orbital rocket on day one. So we're sequencing it honestly:

  1. 01

    Build the community

    Before SkyLakes builds rockets at scale, it's building the people who care about rockets — students, hobbyists, and engineers who show up, ask hard questions, and stay. This is that room.

  2. 02

    Fund the mission with hardware people can hold

    Model rocket kits and sub-components — real revenue from real products, not slide decks. It funds the harder problems and puts rocketry into more hands than a launch ever could on its own.

  3. 03

    Commercial spaceflight

    Everything above builds toward this: SKYLX-S, M, and H flying, reflying, and making sub-₹40Cr LEO access something India's smallsat operators can actually plan around.
